title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
This Week’s Goals

Explain why grid-based planners fail in high-dimensional C-spaces
Describe the sampling-based planning philosophy: probe, don’t discretize
Implement the RRT (Rapidly-exploring Random Tree) algorithm
Extend RRT to RRT* for asymptotically optimal paths
Apply path smoothing to turn tree paths into executable trajectories


Last week we solved path planning on grids with Dijkstra and A. Those work beautifully in 2D/3D. This week we confront the fundamental limitation: grids don’t scale. A 6-DOF arm needs a 6D grid — impossibly large. Sampling-based planners sidestep this by never building the grid at all. Instead, they randomly sample configurations and incrementally build a tree toward the goal. RRT is the foundational algorithm; RRT adds optimality. By the end of today, students will understand when to use grid search vs. sampling-based methods and be able to implement both.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
section: Recap: Grid Search Works in Low Dimensions
text:
Recap: Grid Search Works in Low Dimensions


W11 result: A* on a 2D grid is fast, optimal, complete.
But it depends on discretizing C-space into cells.



Dimension
Cells (100/axis)




2D
\(10^4\)


3D
\(10^6\)


6D
\(10^{12}\)


12D
\(10^{24}\)












Warning


The number of cells grows exponentially with dimension. A 6-DOF robot arm is already infeasible for grid search.




Review the table from W11’s last slide. 100 bins per axis is actually coarse — for a robot arm with 360 degrees of motion per joint, you might want 360 bins. That’s 360^6 ≈ 2 × 10^15 cells for a 6-DOF arm. Even storing one byte per cell would need over a petabyte of memory. And most of those cells are in free space — we’re wasting enormous resources representing empty regions. This is the curse of dimensionality, named by Richard Bellman in 1961.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
The Problem with Grids


Grid planners assume:

We can enumerate all cells (memory)
We can visit relevant cells (time)
Resolution is fine enough to find narrow passages

All three break in high dimensions:

Memory explodes exponentially
Search time explodes with it
Narrow passages require very fine resolution → even more cells





The narrow passage problem is particularly nasty. Imagine two rooms connected by a doorway. In 2D, the doorway is easy to find — a few cells wide. In 6D, the “doorway” in C-space might be a tiny sliver that only a very fine grid would capture. Making the grid finer multiplies memory by a factor of 2^d for each doubling of resolution in d dimensions. Sampling-based planners handle this much better because they don’t commit to a fixed resolution.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
A Different Philosophy


Grid search:

Build a graph from grid cells in configuration space
Search that full graph with Dijkstra/A*

Sampling-based planning:

Keep the configuration space continuous
Test sampled configurations and proposed edges for collision
Add only valid samples/edges to a growing graph or tree





This is the fundamental paradigm shift. Grid planners first create a large discrete approximation of the configuration space, then search that graph. Sampling-based planners keep the space continuous and only create states as needed. A sampled configuration is useful only if it is collision-free, and a connection between two configurations is useful only if the local motion between them is collision-free. We trade the deterministic structure of a full grid for a much smaller graph or tree that grows through the parts of free space the planner actually discovers.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
RRT: The Core Idea


Grow a tree from the start toward the goal:

Pick a random point \(q_{\text{rand}}\) in C-space
Find the nearest node \(q_{\text{near}}\) in the tree
Extend from \(q_{\text{near}}\) toward \(q_{\text{rand}}\) by step size \(\delta\)
If the new point \(q_{\text{new}}\) is collision-free, add it to the tree
Repeat until the tree reaches the goal

The tree rapidly fills the space, biased toward unexplored regions.




RRT was introduced by Steven LaValle in 1998. The key insight is that the nearest-neighbor step creates an implicit bias: nodes in sparsely explored regions have larger Voronoi cells, so random samples are more likely to fall in those regions, causing the tree to expand toward unexplored territory. This is called the Voronoi bias. The step size delta controls the resolution — too large and we might miss obstacles, too small and growth is slow. A typical choice is a fraction of the workspace diameter.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
RRT: Step-by-Step Visualization


Walk through each step on the board. Step 1: the tree has just the start node. A random point is sampled (shown as a hollow circle). The nearest tree node is the start. We extend by delta toward the random point and add the new node (solid circle). Step 2: another random sample. This time the nearest node might be the one we just added. Extend again. Repeat. After many iterations, the tree spans the free space. When a new node lands within delta of the goal, we still check the final segment to the goal before accepting the path. The tree doesn’t follow any predetermined pattern — it’s organic, adapting to the obstacle layout.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
RRT: Interactive Expansion



Use this interactive as a slower version of the pseudocode. Each button press runs one RRT iteration. Students should identify q_rand, the nearest existing tree node, the proposed q_new after steering by delta, and whether the edge is accepted or rejected by collision checking. The key lesson is that failed samples are still part of the algorithm: they do not add nodes, but they show that the planner is testing local motions against obstacles rather than blindly connecting every random point.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
RRT Key Components








Component
What it does
Implementation




random_config()
Uniform sample in C-space
Random point within bounds


nearest(tree, q)
Find closest tree node
Brute force or KD-tree


steer(from, to, δ)
Move from → to by at most δ
Linear interpolation, clip to δ


collision_free(a, b)
Check segment a→b for collisions
Sample points along segment


goal_bias
Occasionally aim directly at goal
Speeds up convergence (typ. 5%)









Tip


Goal biasing is essential in practice. Without it, RRT wanders aimlessly. With 5–10% goal bias, it finds paths much faster.




The nearest-neighbor search is the computational bottleneck. For small trees, brute force (check every node) is fine. For large trees (thousands of nodes), a KD-tree gives O(log n) queries. Collision checking along a segment is done by discretizing the segment into small steps and checking each point — similar to ray casting in W10. The step size delta is a tuning parameter: too large and you collide with thin obstacles, too small and the tree grows slowly.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
Why Does RRT Work?


Voronoi Bias
Nodes in sparsely explored regions have large Voronoi cells.
→ Random samples are more likely to land in those cells.
→ The tree preferentially grows toward unexplored regions.
This is why RRT “rapidly explores” the space — it’s baked into the nearest-neighbor step.




Draw the Voronoi diagram of the tree nodes on the board. Each node “owns” the region of space closer to it than to any other node. When we sample uniformly, the probability that a sample falls in a node’s Voronoi cell is proportional to the cell’s area. Frontier nodes (at the boundary of explored space) have much larger cells than interior nodes. So frontier nodes get selected as q_near more often, and the tree extends outward. This is an elegant emergent property — we never explicitly compute Voronoi cells, but the algorithm behaves as if it does.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
RRT Properties






Strengths



Avoids storing a full grid — practical in higher-dimensional spaces
Probabilistically complete — if a path exists, RRT will find it given enough time
Handles complex obstacle geometries naturally
Easy to implement (~30 lines of core code)










Weaknesses



Not optimal — the first path found is usually jagged and suboptimal
Non-deterministic — different runs give different paths
Can struggle with narrow passages (low probability of sampling through them)
Path quality varies significantly between runs





Probabilistic completeness means: as the number of iterations approaches infinity, the probability of finding a path (if one exists) approaches 1. This is weaker than the deterministic completeness of A* (which always finds a path in finite time if one exists). The non-optimality is the main practical issue — the path follows the tree structure, which is random and jagged. This motivates RRT* and path smoothing, which we’ll cover next.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
The Problem with RRT Paths


RRT finds a path, not the best path.
The tree structure creates unnecessary detours:

Nodes connect to their nearest neighbor at creation time
No rewiring afterward
Path cost can be 2–5× the optimal

Can we fix this?




Show a concrete example: an RRT path that zig-zags around obstacles vs. the straight-line optimal path. The RRT path is valid (collision-free) but much longer than necessary. The issue is that RRT is greedy — each node connects to whatever tree node was nearest when it was created, and that connection is permanent. RRT* fixes this by allowing the tree to rewire itself as new, better connections are discovered.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
RRT*: Asymptotically Optimal RRT

RRT* = RRT + local cost repair: choose the lowest-total-cost parent for \(q_{\text{new}}\), then check nearby tree nodes inside radius \(r\) and let them switch parent if routing through \(q_{\text{new}}\) is cheaper.



The radius r is typically computed as r = gamma * (log(n)/n)^(1/d), where n is the current number of nodes, d is the dimension, and gamma is a constant. This formula ensures we check enough neighbors for optimality but not so many that the algorithm becomes slow. The key theoretical result (Karaman & Frazzoli, 2011) is that with this radius, RRT* is asymptotically optimal: the cost of the best path in the tree converges to the true optimum as n → ∞. In practice, even a few hundred iterations of RRT* produce significantly better paths than basic RRT.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
RRT*: Choose Best Parent
# After q_new is collision-free...
r = rewire_radius(len(nodes))            # shrinks as tree grows
neighbors = nodes_within(nodes, q_new, r) # candidate parents in ball of radius r

# Start with the nearest node as the default parent (basic-RRT choice)
best_parent = q_near
best_cost = cost[q_near] + dist(q_near, q_new)

# Try every neighbor; keep the one giving the lowest cost-to-come
for n in neighbors:
    c = cost[n] + dist(n, q_new)         # cost if we route through n
    if c < best_cost and collision_free(n, q_new, obstacles):
        best_parent = n                  # cheaper AND reachable -> prefer it
        best_cost = c

# Attach q_new to the winning parent and store its cost
nodes[q_new] = best_parent
cost[q_new] = best_cost

The choose-best-parent step is like looking around the neighborhood when you arrive somewhere new and picking the best route to get there. This is the first difference from basic RRT: instead of always attaching q_new to the nearest node, RRT* attaches it to the neighbor that gives the lowest total cost from the start.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
RRT*: Rewire Neighbors
# Now ask: can q_new serve as a BETTER parent for any neighbor?
for n in neighbors:
    new_cost = cost[q_new] + dist(q_new, n)   # cost if n re-parented to q_new

    if (new_cost < cost[n] and                # shortcut found
        collision_free(q_new, n, obstacles)): # and the edge is valid
        nodes[n] = q_new                      # re-parent: n's parent <- q_new
        cost[n] = new_cost                    # update n's cost-to-come

        # n's children inherit the savings, so propagate the delta down the subtree.
        update_descendant_costs(n)






Note


Rewiring lets the tree repair earlier choices as better connections appear.




The rewire step is like telling nearby nodes “it might be faster to go through me.” If the new node creates a shortcut, the tree restructures itself. In production code, changing a parent also requires propagating the cost change to that node’s descendants; the slide names this bookkeeping explicitly so the pseudocode is not misleading. Both operations require collision checks, making RRT* roughly 2-3x slower per iteration than basic RRT. But the path quality improvement is dramatic and worth it in most applications.

Use this table to separate guarantees from practical tradeoffs. RRT is often enough when we only need a feasible path quickly. RRT* spends extra computation improving the tree, so it is the better choice when path quality matters.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
RRT vs RRT*: Cost Convergence




Population view

Median + IQR across 20 random trials
Early RRT rise: more trials find their first path and enter the median
Individual RRT paths do not get worse; after trials have paths, RRT plateaus
RRT* keeps improving by rewiring



Plot is from real measurements: 20 seeds of each planner on the 3-wall maze, 2000 iterations. Median curve plus IQR band shows the population behavior, not one lucky run. RRT typically finds a feasible path around iteration 90 and plateaus near 19.5. RRT* takes a bit longer to find its first path (around iteration 160) because rewiring filters out more candidates per iteration, but the rewiring lets the best-known cost keep decreasing. By iteration 1000 RRT* is essentially at the asymptote (~14.6), about 25% better than RRT.

section: RRT vs RRT*: Watch It Happen
text:
RRT vs RRT*: Watch It Happen



Same scenario as the cost-convergence plot, on the median-cost seed for each planner. Drag the slider to scrub through iterations. Watch the orange RRT path freeze early and the orange RRT* path keep shortening as the tree rewires. The cost label under each panel matches the median curve on the previous slide.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
Why Smooth?


Both RRT and RRT* produce tree paths — sequences of straight segments following tree edges.
Problems:

Unnecessary turns and detours
Not executable by a robot with kinematic constraints
Much longer than needed

Solution: Post-process the path to remove redundant waypoints.




This mirrors the path smoothing we discussed in W11 for grid paths, but it’s even more important for RRT because tree paths are typically more jagged than grid paths. The tree structure imposes arbitrary turns wherever the tree happened to branch. Smoothing can reduce path length by 30-50% in typical scenarios. Two main approaches: shortcutting (try to skip waypoints via line-of-sight) and curve fitting (fit smooth curves through waypoints).

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
Shortcut Smoothing


Algorithm:

Pick two random waypoints \(w_i\) and \(w_j\) on the path (\(j > i + 1\))
Check if the straight line \(w_i \to w_j\) is collision-free
If yes, replace the sub-path \(w_i \to \ldots \to w_j\) with the direct segment
Repeat for \(N\) iterations

Simple, effective, and fast.
Each successful shortcut removes unnecessary detours.




This is a randomized algorithm — we randomly pick pairs of waypoints and try to shortcut them. The order doesn’t matter because any valid shortcut reduces path length. Typically 50-200 iterations are enough to remove most redundancy. The collision check is the same as in RRT: discretize the segment and check each point. An alternative deterministic approach is greedy smoothing (from W11): start at the beginning, find the farthest visible waypoint, jump there, repeat. The randomized approach is often better for complex paths because it can find shortcuts that greedy smoothing misses.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
Planner Choice Cheat Sheet


Low-dimensional maps



Scenario
Planner




2D mobile robot
A* on grid


3D drone
A* or RRT


Known occupancy grid
A* first



Use grid search when the state space is small enough to discretize.

High-dimensional C-space



Scenario
Planner




6-DOF arm
RRT / RRT*


Real-time replanning
RRT + smoothing


High-quality path
RRT* + smoothing


Narrow passages
bidirectional RRT



Use sampling when a grid would explode in memory or time.


This decision table is the practical takeaway. Students should be able to look at a planning problem and immediately choose the right algorithm family. The dimension of the C-space is the primary factor. For 2D, always use A* — it’s faster and gives optimal paths. For 3D, it depends on the map complexity and real-time requirements. For anything higher, sampling-based is the only option. Bidirectional RRT (grow a tree from start and from goal, connect when they meet) is particularly effective for narrow passages because both trees can find opposite ends of the passage.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
Bidirectional RRT


Grow two trees simultaneously:

Tree A from the start
Tree B from the goal

After each extension, try to connect the two trees.
Advantages:

Finds paths faster (searches from both ends)
Much better at narrow passages
Connection attempts are like aggressive goal biasing





Bidirectional RRT is the most commonly used variant in practice. The two trees meet in the middle, which dramatically reduces the expected number of iterations. For narrow passages, growing from the goal side is crucial — a single tree from the start might never find the narrow entrance, but if another tree is growing from the other side of the passage, they meet inside it. RRT-Connect (Kuffner & LaValle, 2000) is a popular variant that greedily extends toward the other tree, not just one step at a time.

The Full Planning Pipeline

    I --> P{"Dimension?"}
    P -->|"2D/3D"| AS["A* Grid Search<br/>(W11)"]
    P -->|"≥ 4D"| RR["RRT / RRT*<br/>(W12)"]
    AS --> SM["Path Smoothing"]
    RR --> SM
    SM --> T["Trajectory<br/>(W06)"]
    T --> K["Kinematic<br/>Controller<br/>(W09)"]
    style P fill:#f39c12,color:#fff,stroke:#c0392b
    style SM fill:#8e44ad,color:#fff,stroke:#6c3483













Tip


Planning produces a path; smoothing, timing, and control turn it into motion.




This ties together everything from the course. The occupancy map from W10 feeds into obstacle inflation (C-space from W11). Based on the dimension, we choose grid search or sampling-based planning. Both produce a raw path that gets smoothed. The smoothed waypoints go to the trajectory generator from W06 (polynomial interpolation), and the trajectory is tracked by the kinematic controller from W09. This is essentially the full autonomy stack for a mobile robot. Real systems like ROS’s move_base follow exactly this pipeline.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
Key Takeaways

Curse of dimensionality makes grid-based planning infeasible above 3–4 dimensions
RRT grows a tree by random sampling — probabilistically complete, practical in high dimensions
Voronoi bias gives RRT its exploration property: frontier nodes grow faster
RRT* adds rewiring for asymptotic optimality — converges to the shortest path
Path smoothing (shortcutting) removes tree artifacts, essential for executable paths
Decision rule: use A* for 2D/3D grids, RRT/RRT* for higher dimensions







Note


Next week: The robot has a path — but where is it? Localization (W13): estimating the robot’s pose from noisy sensor data.




Recap the key ideas. Emphasize the decision rule — this is what students should take away for their projects. Also note the progression: W10 gave us maps, W11 gave us grid-based planning, W12 gave us sampling-based planning, and W13 will address the question “but where am I on this map?” The final piece of the autonomy puzzle.

title: Week 13: Localization — Where Am I?
text:
This Week’s Goals

Explain why wheel odometry alone drifts and why localization is a separate problem
Frame localization as a belief \(\text{bel}(x_t)\) over robot poses — not a single estimate
Apply the Bayes filter: motion update (predict) and sensor update (correct)
Implement the particle filter (Monte Carlo Localization): sample, weight, resample
Choose between Kalman filter and particle filter based on the problem structure
Recognize when the map is also unknown — and meet SLAM (EKF-SLAM, FastSLAM, pose-graph + loop closure)


Last week’s planners (W11 A, W12 RRT) handed the robot a path. But a path is in map* coordinates — to follow it, the robot must know where it is on the map. W09 gave us kinematic models that let us predict pose changes from wheel speeds, and W10 gave us sensors (LiDAR, vision) and an occupancy grid. Today we close the loop: combine motion predictions with sensor measurements to maintain a probabilistic estimate of pose. By the end, students should understand why localization must be probabilistic, recognize the Bayes filter behind every common localization algorithm, and be able to trace one cycle of a particle filter by hand.

title: Week 13: Localization — Where Am I?
section: A Path Without a Position is Useless
text:
A Path Without a Position is Useless


W11 and W12 gave us paths in map coordinates.
To execute one, the robot needs the answer to two questions at every step:

Where am I on the map right now?
Where is the next waypoint relative to me?

Without (1), even a perfect plan turns into a random walk.
Localization = continually estimating the robot pose \(x_t = (x,\, y,\, \theta)\) from:

A map (built in W10) — known occupancy grid
Control inputs \(u_t = (v,\,\omega)\) — commanded linear & angular speed
Sensor measurements \(z_t\) — e.g. a LiDAR scan at time \(t\)

Subscript \(t\) throughout = “at time step \(t\)”.




Set the scene by reminding students that W11/W12 produced waypoints on a map. The map is fixed; the robot moves. The controller from W09 needs an error signal (goal pose minus current pose) — and “current pose” is what localization provides. Without a good pose estimate, the controller is steering blind. Today we focus on the case where the map is known. Building the map and localizing simultaneously is SLAM, which is a graduate course on its own.

title: Week 13: Localization — Where Am I?
text:
First Attempt: Wheel Odometry


From W09 the unicycle model gives:
\[
\dot{x} = v\cos\theta,\quad \dot{y} = v\sin\theta,\quad \dot{\theta} = \omega
\]
\(\dot{x},\dot{y}\): world-frame velocities (m/s) · \(\theta\): heading (rad) · \(v,\omega\): commanded linear and angular speed.
Integrate the commanded \((v,\omega)\) over time → predicted pose. This is dead reckoning: pose from controls alone.
So why isn’t this enough?







Warning


Every step has a small error:

Wheel slip
Tire diameter drift
Uneven floor
Encoder quantization
Unmodelled dynamics

Errors accumulate without bound.





Dead reckoning gives us a prediction but never a correction. Even with high-quality encoders, a typical differential-drive robot loses a few percent of its translation and accumulates a fraction of a degree of heading error per meter. Over a 50-meter trajectory, that easily becomes one or two meters off — enough to drive into a wall. This is why odometry alone has never been the answer for serious mobile robots.

title: Week 13: Localization — Where Am I?
text:
Odometry Drift in Action







Warning


Position error grows roughly linearly with distance traveled; heading error grows even faster after turns.




This figure is generated from a simulation: a true robot drives a rectangular loop and returns to start, while dead reckoning integrates noisy controls. After one lap of about 30 meters the dead-reckoning estimate is half a meter off, and on the second lap that error doubles. There is no mechanism in pure odometry to remove this error — only the next wall sighting or landmark observation can do that. This motivates sensor fusion: combining the (drifting but smooth) odometry with (noisy but bounded) sensor measurements.

title: Week 13: Localization — Where Am I?
text:
The Cure: Use the Sensors


The map and the LiDAR/camera give us a second source of information:

Predict where I should be from \((v,\omega)\)
Compare the predicted scan with the actual scan
Correct the pose so the two agree

This is sensor fusion — and the principled way to do it is probabilistic.
We will not maintain a single pose. We will maintain a belief — a probability distribution over poses.




Each information source is incomplete on its own. Odometry is smooth but drifts. LiDAR matched to the map gives bounded error but is jumpy and noisy. The Bayes filter is the mathematical machinery that fuses the two so their strengths cancel each other’s weaknesses. Probability is not optional here — the robot is uncertain about its pose, and ignoring that uncertainty leads to overconfident, brittle behavior.

title: Week 13: Localization — Where Am I?
text:
Belief: a Distribution Over Poses


\[\text{bel}(x_t) \;=\; p(x_t \,\mid\, z_{1:t},\; u_{1:t})\]
Read aloud: “probability the robot is at pose \(x_t\) given every measurement and every control so far.”

\(x_t\) — candidate robot pose at time \(t\)
\(z_{1:t}\) — measurements \(z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_t\)
\(u_{1:t}\) — controls \(u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_t\)
\(p(A \mid B)\) — probability of \(A\) knowing \(B\)

Sharp = confident · flat = no idea · multimodal = several places at once.




The phrase “the robot is at (3.2, 4.1)” is misleading — the robot is at some pose, and from the available data we have a belief about which poses are plausible. A multimodal belief is common at startup (“am I in hallway A or hallway B — they look identical”), and a key advantage of particle filters over Kalman filters is the ability to represent these multimodal beliefs naturally.

title: Week 13: Localization — Where Am I?
section: The Bayes Filter: Two Steps Per Cycle
text:
The Bayes Filter: Two Steps Per Cycle


1. Motion update (predict) — belief spreads:
\[\overline{\text{bel}}(x_t) \;=\; \int p(x_t \mid u_t,\, x_{t-1})\,\text{bel}(x_{t-1})\,\mathrm{d}x_{t-1}\]

\(\overline{\text{bel}}(x_t)\) — predicted belief (bar = before measurement)
\(p(x_t \mid u_t, x_{t-1})\) — motion model
\(\int \mathrm{d}x_{t-1}\) — sum over every possible previous pose

2. Sensor update (correct) — belief sharpens:
\[\text{bel}(x_t) \;=\; \eta\,\, p(z_t \mid x_t)\,\overline{\text{bel}}(x_t)\]

\(p(z_t \mid x_t)\) — measurement model
\(\eta\) — normalization constant so the belief integrates to 1





This is the single most important pair of equations in mobile robotics. The motion model p(x_t | u_t, x_{t-1}) says “if I was here and applied this control, where might I be now?” — it captures process noise. The measurement model p(z_t | x_t) says “if I were at this pose, how likely is the scan I just saw?” — it captures sensor noise. The integral and the multiplication are the only operations involved; everything else (Kalman filter, particle filter, histogram filter) is a different way of representing and computing these two operations.

title: Week 13: Localization — Where Am I?
text:
The Bayes Filter: Algorithm


# bel_prev: pose -> prob   |  motion_model(x, u, x') -> p(x|u, x')
# u_t: control this step   |  sensor_model(z, x)    -> p(z|x)
# z_t: latest measurement

def bayes_filter(bel_prev, u_t, z_t, motion_model, sensor_model):
    # ① PREDICT — push belief through motion model
    bel_bar = {}
    for x_t in poses:
        bel_bar[x_t] = sum(
            motion_model(x_t, u_t, x_prev) * bel_prev[x_prev]
            for x_prev in poses)

    # ② CORRECT — re-weight by measurement likelihood
    bel = {x_t: sensor_model(z_t, x_t) * bel_bar[x_t]
           for x_t in poses}

    # ③ NORMALIZE — eta so probabilities sum to 1
    eta = 1.0 / sum(bel.values())
    return {x_t: eta * b for x_t, b in bel.items()}

Note


Every common localization method (Kalman filter, EKF, particle filter, histogram filter) is a way of representing \(\text{bel}\) and computing these two updates efficiently.




Walk students through the diagram in sync with the code. Start at the top-left: the previous belief bel(x_{t-1}) and the control u_t both feed into the PREDICT block. Out comes bel̄(x_t) — the predicted belief, still uncorrected. That feeds into CORRECT along with the new measurement z_t. The result is unnormalized, so we multiply by η to get bel(x_t). The dashed arrow back to the top reminds students that this output becomes the next cycle’s input — the filter runs forever. The numbered circles ①②③ in the diagram match the comments in the code so students can map between them. Emphasize the orange external inputs (controls and measurements) and the blue belief states; the algorithm’s job is to consume one and one to update the other. The naive implementation above only works if x_t is discrete and small (a “histogram filter”). In continuous space the sums become integrals and are intractable. Kalman filters assume everything is Gaussian and linear, reducing the filter to a few matrix operations. Particle filters represent the belief with samples, sidestepping the integral entirely. EKFs linearize nonlinear models around the current estimate. The choice of representation drives everything else.

title: Week 13: Localization — Where Am I?
text:
A Worked 1-D Example


Scenario: Robot lives on a corridor with 10 cells. There are three doors.

Prior: Uniform belief — no idea where the robot is.
Sensor: Robot reports “I see a door.”
Motion: Robot moves +1 cell.
Sensor: Robot reports “I see a door” again.

After step 2 the belief becomes trimodal (the three doors). After step 4 the only consistent location is the one door that has another door to its right.
Two scans, one motion → unique pose.




This is Sebastian Thrun’s classic corridor example. It demonstrates two ideas at once: (1) a single measurement is rarely enough — the prior matters, (2) combining measurements with motion can resolve ambiguity even when each individual measurement is uninformative. In simulation a sequence of just a few “door / no door” observations is enough to localize globally, even without any pose continuity assumption. Real robots do the same thing with LiDAR scans against the occupancy grid.

title: Week 13: Localization — Where Am I?
text:
Why Particles?


The Bayes filter is exact but the integrals are intractable in \((x, y, \theta)\).

Kalman filter — fast, but Gaussian / linear only
Histogram filter — general, but cells explode in 3-D
Particle filter — represent belief with samples

A particle \(x_t^{[i]} = (x^{[i]},\, y^{[i]},\, \theta^{[i]})\) is one guess of where the robot is. Superscript \([i]\) is the particle index (\(i = 1, \ldots, N\)).

\(N\) — number of particles (we choose this)
Sample density ≈ belief density
No assumption about shape — handles multimodal beliefs naturally





Each particle is a complete pose hypothesis: an (x, y, θ) point that says “the robot might be here.” A cloud of 1000 particles spread over a meter says “we think the robot is in this area, with this spread.” When the cloud collapses to a tight cluster, the filter is confident. When it splits into separate clusters, the filter is honestly admitting that more than one pose is consistent with the data. This is the same idea as the curse of dimensionality from W12: don’t discretize the whole space, just probe the parts that matter.

title: Week 13: Localization — Where Am I?
text:
Three Steps, Repeated Forever









Step
Particle operation
Bayes filter equivalent




1. Predict
Move each particle through the noisy motion model
Motion update


2. Weight
Score each particle by \(w^{[i]} = p(z_t \mid x_t^{[i]})\)
Sensor update


3. Resample
Draw \(N\) new particles with replacement, probability \(\propto w^{[i]}\)
Belief normalization



Where \(w^{[i]}\) is the weight of particle \(i\) — how well its pose explains the current sensor reading \(z_t\). High weight = “if the robot were here, this scan makes sense.”

The cycle: predict, weight, resample. Each step is short to describe but each one hides important detail. Predict adds noise — without it all particles march in lockstep and the filter cannot recover from errors. Weight uses the measurement model — a likelihood, not a probability, so we can compare relative scores without computing a partition function. Resample focuses computation on plausible regions, but if you resample too aggressively you lose diversity (particle deprivation).

title: Week 13: Localization — Where Am I?
text:
Step 1: Predict — Push Each Particle


# v, w : commanded linear / angular speed
# dt   : step duration (s)   | theta: heading (rad)
# nx, ny, nth : per-particle motion-noise samples
for i in range(N):
    x_pred  = particles[i].x     + (v*cos(theta) + nx) * dt
    y_pred  = particles[i].y     + (v*sin(theta) + ny) * dt
    th_pred = particles[i].theta + (w + nth)           * dt
    particles[i] = (x_pred, y_pred, th_pred)
nx, ny, nth are independent draws from a zero-mean Gaussian motion-noise model.
Without noise the cloud only drifts; it cannot spread to represent growing uncertainty.




The motion noise model is the single biggest knob in a particle filter. Too little noise and the cloud is overconfident — particles cannot reach the true pose, so the next sensor update kills them all and the filter “dies” (all weights zero). Too much noise and the cloud explodes and the filter never converges. A good rule of thumb: model both translational and rotational noise proportional to the commanded motion (a long arc has more uncertainty than a short straight line).

title: Week 13: Localization — Where Am I?
section: Step 2: Weight — Compare to the Measurement
text:
Step 2: Weight — Compare to the Measurement


Score each particle by the likelihood it would have produced \(z_t\). For a LiDAR scan against the known map:
# z_actual : real scan (vector of K beam ranges, m)
# raycast(map, pose) -> expected beams from that pose
# sigma    : assumed beam-noise std-dev (m)
for i in range(N):
    z_expected = raycast(map, particles[i])  # from W10
    err        = z_actual - z_expected       # per-beam residual
    weights[i] = exp(-0.5 * (err / sigma)**2).prod()
Particles that “see what the robot sees” get high weight; those that don’t, near-zero.




The expected scan z_expected is obtained by simulating the LiDAR from the particle’s pose against the known map — this is the ray-casting we built in W10. We compare expected and actual reading-by-reading, treat the residuals as Gaussian, and multiply the per-beam likelihoods (assuming independence between beams). In practice we use the log-likelihood to avoid numerical underflow when N is large. Particles in walls — where ray-casting would yield zero range — automatically get zero weight, so the filter never returns “the robot is inside an obstacle.”

title: Week 13: Localization — Where Am I?
text:
Step 3: Resample — Keep the Plausible


Draw \(N\) new particles with replacement, with the chance of picking particle \(i\) proportional to its weight \(w^{[i]}\).
# weights / weights.sum() : normalized probabilities (one per particle)
# replace=True            : same particle may be chosen many times
indices = np.random.choice(
    N, size=N, replace=True,
    p=weights / weights.sum()
)
particles = particles[indices]
weights[:] = 1.0 / N             # reset to uniform
Effect: high-weight particles produce many copies; low-weight particles disappear.






Warning


Resampling every step destroys diversity. Use low-variance resampling and resample only when needed.







Resampling is where the particle cloud concentrates onto plausible regions. Two practical refinements: (1) Low-variance (systematic) resampling — instead of N independent draws, take one random offset and step through the CDF evenly. This dramatically reduces resampling variance for the same expected behavior. (2) Effective sample size — only resample when N_eff = 1 / sum(w_i^2) drops below a threshold (say N/2). This avoids unnecessary loss of diversity when the weights are already approximately uniform.

title: Week 13: Localization — Where Am I?
text:
Particle Filter: Pseudocode
# particles     : N pose hypotheses [(x, y, theta), ...]
# u_t           : control this step, e.g. (v, omega)
# z_t           : measurement (LiDAR scan: K beam ranges)
# map_          : known occupancy grid (W10)
# motion_noise  : std-devs for the motion model
# sigma         : assumed LiDAR beam noise (m)

def particle_filter(particles, u_t, z_t, map_, motion_noise, sigma):
    N = len(particles)
    weights = np.empty(N)

    # ① Predict — sample next pose from motion model
    for i in range(N):
        particles[i] = motion_model_sample(particles[i], u_t, motion_noise)

    # ② Weight — likelihood of z_t under each particle
    for i in range(N):
        z_expected = raycast(map_, particles[i])
        weights[i] = gaussian_likelihood(z_t, z_expected, sigma)

    # ③ Resample — only when diversity drops (N_eff = 1 / Σ w_i²)
    weights /= weights.sum()
    if effective_sample_size(weights) < N / 2:
        particles = low_variance_resample(particles, weights)

    return particles

The whole filter is about 20 lines of substance. The expensive bit is the ray-cast inside the weight step — for N=1000 particles and 360-beam LiDAR, that’s 360,000 ray-casts per cycle. Real implementations downsample beams (use every 10th), reduce N once converged, and use space-partitioning data structures over the map. The structure of the algorithm, though, is exactly what’s shown above.

title: Week 13: Localization — Where Am I?
text:
Global Localization (Kidnapped Robot)


Initial condition: robot is dropped into a known map with no idea where it is.

Initialize \(N\) particles uniformly over the free space of the map.
Run predict / weight / resample as usual.
After a few scans the cloud collapses onto the true pose.

This is the famous Monte Carlo Localization result — and it works because the particle filter naturally handles multimodal beliefs.




This demo (figure shows iterations 0, 5, 20, 50) is the canonical “wow” moment for MCL. A Kalman filter cannot do this — it has a single Gaussian belief that can only represent one mode, so an initial uniform belief is impossible to express. Particle filters handle it for free. The convergence rate depends on how distinguishable the map is — a featureless room is hard, a corridor with three offset doors is easy. Sebastian Thrun’s lab demonstrated this on a real wheeled robot at Carnegie Mellon in 1999, and it became the standard mobile robot localization technique within a decade.

title: Week 13: Localization — Where Am I?
text:
How Many Particles?





Phase
Typical \(N\)
Why




Global localization
5 000 – 50 000
Cover the whole map


Tracking a known pose
200 – 1 000
Tight cloud, low compute


Recovery (kidnapped)
bump back up
Re-spread quickly



KLD sampling: adapt \(N\) online so the discretization error of the particle cloud stays below a target — a few thousand particles in cluttered regions, a few hundred when localized.






Tip


Practical AMCL settings (ros-navigation): min_particles=500, max_particles=2000.







A common student mistake is to fix N=1000 forever and wonder why global localization fails: 1000 particles over a 20×20 m room at 0.1 m spacing already underfills the floor plan, before we even consider orientation. The standard practice is to start large, let the filter converge, and shed particles as the belief tightens. KLD (Kullback-Leibler Distance) sampling is the formal version of this: pick N just large enough that the particle distribution approximates the true belief to a chosen tolerance.

title: Week 13: Localization — Where Am I?
text:
Two Failure Modes


Particle deprivation
Too few particles in the right region → the true pose has zero weight every step → filter cannot recover.
Fix:

Increase \(N\)
Inject random samples each step (the augmented MCL trick)
Larger motion noise so the cloud spreads


Sample impoverishment
After many resampling rounds, only a few unique particles remain — diversity collapses even if \(N\) is large.
Fix:

Resample only when effective sample size is low
Use low-variance resampling
Add a small jitter (“roughening”) after resampling








Warning


Both failure modes look the same on a plot — a tiny, confident cloud sitting in the wrong place. The filter never reports an error; it just diverges silently.




Particle deprivation and sample impoverishment are two distinct problems that get conflated in introductory treatments. Deprivation = “no particles where they should be” (a sampling problem). Impoverishment = “too many duplicate particles” (a diversity problem). Both lead to overconfident, wrong estimates. The standard defense is augmented MCL: every step, replace a small fraction (say 1%) of particles with random samples from the map. This costs almost nothing and prevents both failures from being permanent.

title: Week 13: Localization — Where Am I?
text:
Kalman vs Particle Filter









Kalman filter
Particle filter




Belief shape
Gaussian only
Arbitrary (multimodal OK)


Models
Linear (EKF: linearized)
Any motion / sensor model


Cost per step
\(\mathcal{O}(d^3)\)
\(\mathcal{O}(N\cdot\text{raycast})\)


Global localization
Cannot represent it
Natural — uniform prior


Tuning
\(Q, R\) matrices
\(N\) + motion / sensor noise


Use when…
Smooth, well-modeled, unimodal
Multimodal, nonlinear, ambiguous



\(d\) — state dim (e.g. 3 for \((x,y,\theta)\)) · \(N\) — # particles · \(Q\) — process-noise cov · \(R\) — measurement-noise cov.






Tip


Many production systems run both: a particle filter for global localization, then hand off to an EKF once the belief is unimodal.




This comparison is what students should walk away with. Kalman filters win on small, smooth problems with Gaussian noise — IMU integration, tracking a single object with a camera. Particle filters win when ambiguity exists — global localization, multi-target tracking, terrain-based navigation. The hybrid pattern is increasingly common: use the right tool for each phase. ROS’s amcl package is the canonical particle-filter implementation; robot_localization is the canonical EKF/UKF package. Both are used in the same stack.

The localizer tells the planner where the robot is and tells the controller what pose to track toward. Without the localizer, the planner cannot start and the controller cannot steer. With everything in place, the robot can be dropped onto a known map, find itself, plan a route, and execute it — the full stack we’ve been building since W09.

Sensor model (std-dev \(\sigma = 1.0\) m, \(\propto\) = “proportional to”): \[w^{[i]} \;\propto\; \exp\!\left[-\tfrac12 \left(\tfrac{z_t - (10 - x^{[i]})}{\sigma}\right)^2\right]\]

Walk through this on the board. The trick is that after the motion update, the predicted distance-to-wall for each particle is 10 - (x + 1). The actual reading 3.0 corresponds to “the robot is at x=7.” So particle 3 (which is at x=8 → predicted x=9 → predicted reading 1) is way off. Particle 2 (x=5 → predicted x=6 → predicted reading 4) is the closest match. Particle 1 (x=2 → predicted x=3 → predicted reading 7) is also off. After weighting and resampling, the cloud should concentrate near particle 2’s region — and at the next cycle that cluster keeps refining.

title: Week 13: Localization — Where Am I?
text:
Key Takeaways

Odometry drifts unboundedly — localization must fuse motion predictions with sensor measurements.
Belief over poses, not a single pose: the Bayes filter is the principled framework.
Particle filter = represent the belief by \(N\) samples; predict, weight, resample.
Motion noise is mandatory — without it the cloud cannot represent growing uncertainty.
MCL handles global localization for free because particles can represent multimodal beliefs.
Decision rule: Kalman for unimodal/Gaussian, particle filter for multimodal or strongly nonlinear.
SLAM = same Bayes filter on a joint pose+map state. EKF-SLAM, FastSLAM, pose-graph + loop closure are the three pillars.







Note


Next week: Final project presentations and course review. You now have everything you need to build a full mobile autonomy stack — perception (W10), localization (W13), planning (W11/W12), trajectory (W06), and control (W09).




Tie it all back. The Bayes filter is the most reusable idea today — it appears in computer vision (tracking), control (state estimation), graphics (Kalman smoothing), and beyond. Particle filters specifically are the dominant method whenever the belief is multimodal or the models are nonlinear. After this week the autonomy stack from W09 onward is conceptually complete: a real robot, given a map, can find itself, plan a route, and drive it. Final project demos next week show all five components working together.

title: Week 13: Localization — Where Am I?
text:
Drop the Map Assumption


Everything so far assumed the map is known.
What if the robot is exploring an unknown building? It has to build the map while it drives.
But:

To localize, the robot needs a map
To map, the robot needs to know its pose

SLAM — Simultaneous Localization And Mapping — solves both at the same time.




SLAM is what lets a Roomba, a warehouse AGV, or a self-driving car operate in environments where no human pre-built a map. Conceptually it is the same Bayes filter we just covered, but the state now contains both the robot’s pose AND a representation of the environment. Hugh Durrant-Whyte and John Leonard formalized the SLAM problem in the late 1980s; it became practical with EKF-SLAM in the 1990s and then exploded after FastSLAM (2002) and modern graph-based methods around 2010. Today SLAM is the backbone of every commercial mobile-robot product.

title: Week 13: Localization — Where Am I?
text:
The Joint State


Augment the state with the map. For point landmarks \(\ell_1, \ldots, \ell_M\):
\[\xi_t \;=\; \begin{bmatrix} x_t \\ \ell_1 \\ \ell_2 \\ \vdots \\ \ell_M \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \dim(\xi_t) = 3 + 2M\]

\(\xi_t\) — the joint SLAM state at time \(t\) (Greek “xi”)
\(x_t\) — robot pose \((x, y, \theta)\)
\(\ell_j = (\ell_{j,x}, \ell_{j,y})\) — 2-D position of landmark \(j\)
\(M\) — number of landmarks seen so far (grows as new landmarks are observed)

Full vs online SLAM:

Full SLAM estimates the entire trajectory \(x_{0:t}\) plus the map
Online SLAM only keeps the current pose \(x_t\) plus the map (cheaper, what most filters do)





The Greek letter ξ (xi) is the conventional SLAM notation for the joint state — Thrun/Burgard/Fox use it throughout Probabilistic Robotics. The key insight is that the state itself grows every time we observe a previously unseen landmark, which makes SLAM very different from classical filtering. Full SLAM keeps the entire history of poses, which is essential for global re-optimization (pose-graph SLAM); online SLAM marginalizes out past poses, which is cheaper but loses information.

title: Week 13: Localization — Where Am I?
text:
EKF-SLAM: Augment the Kalman State


Apply the Extended Kalman Filter to the joint state \(\xi_t\):

Belief = a single Gaussian over \(\xi_t\)
Mean \(\mu_t\): best estimate of pose and every landmark
Covariance \(\Sigma_t\): uncertainty and all cross-correlations

Why correlations matter: if the robot is uncertain about its pose, then every landmark it places is uncertain by the same amount. Observing one landmark improves the estimate of every other landmark through the covariance.
Cost: \(\mathcal{O}(M^2)\) per update — \(\Sigma_t\) is \((3{+}2M) \times (3{+}2M)\).







Note


Symbols

\(\mu_t\) — mean of the Gaussian belief over \(\xi_t\)
\(\Sigma_t\) — covariance matrix of \(\xi_t\)
EKF — Extended Kalman Filter (linearizes nonlinear motion / sensor models)










Warning


EKF-SLAM scales poorly past a few hundred landmarks and assumes a unimodal Gaussian belief.





EKF-SLAM was the dominant approach in the 1990s-2000s. The off-diagonal blocks of the covariance matrix encode that the robot pose and the landmarks are coupled — this is what makes loop closure work even in the EKF setting. Once the robot sees a landmark it has seen before, the correlations cause the entire trajectory to re-organize. The quadratic cost is the killing weakness; on a large map with thousands of features it becomes too slow.

title: Week 13: Localization — Where Am I?
section: FastSLAM: a Particle Filter for SLAM
text:
FastSLAM: a Particle Filter for SLAM


Key insight (Murphy 1999, Montemerlo 2002): if the robot pose history \(x_{0:t}\) were known exactly, then the landmarks \(\ell_j\) would be conditionally independent of each other.
→ Build a particle filter over the pose, and let each particle carry its own little map.
For particle \(i\) at time \(t\):

\(x_t^{[i]}\) — pose hypothesis (like W13’s PF)
\(\{\mathcal{N}(\mu_{j}^{[i]}, \Sigma_{j}^{[i]})\}_{j=1}^{M}\) — one tiny EKF per landmark, independent

Three steps per cycle:

Predict pose for each particle (same as MCL)
Weight particle by the likelihood of \(z_t\) given its map
Update that particle’s landmark EKFs with the new measurement; resample





FastSLAM is the natural marriage of the particle filter we just built and SLAM. Conditioned on a specific pose trajectory, the landmark estimates decouple — so instead of one giant 2M+3 dimensional Gaussian, we keep N small per-particle Gaussians. The total cost is O(N · M log M) with a tree structure, dramatically beating EKF-SLAM’s O(M^2). FastSLAM also inherits the multimodal-belief strength of particle filters, so it can handle ambiguity in data association (“which landmark did I just see?”). It powered the famous Stanley win at the 2005 DARPA Grand Challenge.

title: Week 13: Localization — Where Am I?
text:
Pose-Graph SLAM and Loop Closure


Pose-graph SLAM treats the problem as a graph:

Nodes — robot poses \(x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_t\) (one per time step)
Edges — relative-pose constraints

Odometry edges: from controls \(u_t\) between consecutive poses
Loop-closure edges: when the robot re-observes a place it has seen before


Optimization minimizes the total constraint error:
\[\min_{x_{0:t}} \;\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}} \big\| z_{ij} - h(x_i, x_j) \big\|^2_{\Omega_{ij}}\]

\(\mathcal{E}\) — set of edges in the graph
\(z_{ij}\) — measured relative pose on edge \((i,j)\)
\(h(x_i, x_j)\) — predicted relative pose from current estimates
\(\Omega_{ij}\) — information (inverse-covariance) weight of that edge

Loop closure is the magic: one new edge can re-organize the whole trajectory.




This is the modern method behind almost every state-of-the-art SLAM system: Google Cartographer, ORB-SLAM, LIO-SAM, RTAB-Map. Pose-graph SLAM separates the problem into “build constraints in real time” (the front end) and “optimize them whenever a loop closure arrives” (the back end). The optimization is a sparse nonlinear least squares — libraries like g2o, GTSAM, and Ceres make it solvable in milliseconds even for thousands of poses. The dramatic improvement at loop closure is the headline result: a robot that has drifted a meter over a 200-meter loop snaps back to the correct trajectory the instant it recognizes the start of the loop.

Where SLAM fits in this course:

W10 taught the map representation (occupancy grid)

SLAM = the natural extension when you don’t have one







Tip


For your final project: if the map is known, use W13’s particle filter. If you must explore, drop in gmapping (ROS) or RTAB-Map — both expose the same /map and /tf interfaces.





This slide is the practical takeaway. Mobile robotics today rarely requires students to implement SLAM from scratch — robust libraries exist for every common sensor stack. What they do need is the conceptual model from the previous slides: pose + map joint state, the Bayes filter machinery, pose-graph with loop closure. Once they understand those concepts they can read the documentation of any modern SLAM package and know what knobs to turn. For the final project, encourage anyone exploring unknown environments to use ROS gmapping (2-D LiDAR) or RTAB-Map (camera) rather than writing custom code.

title: Week 13: Localization — Where Am I?
text:
How These Methods Relate


Everything we name today comes from one equation — the Bayes filter — combined with two choices:
Choice 1 — Shape of the belief

Kalman / EKF — one Gaussian
Histogram filter — a grid (mentioned, not used)
Particle filter — \(N\) samples

Choice 2 — Problem to solve

Localization — pose only, map known
SLAM — pose and map together

Every method we discuss is one cell of the matrix on the right.










Kalman family (one Gaussian)
Particle family (\(N\) samples)




Localization (known map)
EKF localization
MCL ← Parts 2–3


SLAM (unknown map)
EKF-SLAM
FastSLAM









Note


Pose-graph SLAM is the odd one out — it’s an optimization on the full trajectory, not a per-step filter. Think of it as the “smoother” alternative to filtering. Covered later in Part 5.









Tip


MCL = “particle filter applied to localization.” It’s not a separate algorithm — it’s a use case.





Use this slide as a navigator. Students should be able to point at any term we’ve used so far (Bayes filter, Kalman, EKF, particle filter, MCL) and any term in the upcoming SLAM section (EKF-SLAM, FastSLAM, pose-graph) and locate it on this map. The key insight: there are not “many algorithms” — there is one Bayes filter, two belief representations we care about (Gaussian and samples), and two problems (localization vs SLAM). Every named method is one (representation, problem) pair. Pose-graph SLAM is the exception because it’s a smoother (optimizes the whole trajectory at once) rather than a filter (one-step recursive update); mention this briefly but don’t dwell on it — it gets its own slide later.
